comparison: Both evaluate claims C32-C33 about residual sensitivity in highly confident non-noticers. OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as strengthening the main finding, while peer reviewers find it UNSUPPORTED, arguing the result likely reflects measurement error from subjects who misunderstood confidence scales. This represents fundamental disagreement on data quality.

Both address claims C8, C20, C62-C63 about theoretical implications challenging the orthodox view of IB. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED (with caveats about interpretation), while peer reviewers find them UNSUPPORTED, characterizing the challenge as modest (~8% overestimate) rather than fundamental, and questioning whether above-chance performance proves conscious awareness versus subliminal processing.

Both evaluate claims C55-C56 about whether residual sensitivity reflects conscious versus unconscious processing. OpenEval rates this UNCERTAIN, acknowledging it remains interpretive rather than empirically demonstrated. Peer reviewers also rate it UNCERTAIN, suggesting above-chance performance could reflect subliminal priming analogous to masked priming studies, highlighting fundamental ambiguity about what forced-choice performance indicates.

Both address claims C4, C15-C17 about the theoretical motivation and critique of yes/no questions in prior IB research. OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as well-grounded in psychophysics literature. Peer reviewers find it UNSUPPORTED, arguing the authors misrepresent the field by creating a straw-man, citing 18 studies (including some the authors cite) that use multiple questions rather than simple yes/no procedures.

OpenEval R4 addresses claims C22, C46-C49 about methodological critiques of prior literature, finding them SUPPORTED. Peer R4 overlaps on C46-C48 but finds the characterization UNSUPPORTED, arguing it's a straw-man since most studies don't just use yes/no methods. This represents disagreement on how accurately the authors characterize existing literature.

Both evaluate methodological claims including large sample sizes (C23), novel analytical approach (C24, C44), and pre-registration (C66). Both find these SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes these as methodological strengths, while peer reviewers explicitly compliment the massive data collection, signal detection measures, and 'super subject' approach as important contributions to the field.

OpenEval R5 includes claim C42 about adherence to canonical paradigms as SUPPORTED. Peer R5 addresses C42-C43 about lack of control conditions, finding this UNSUPPORTED with weak justification, arguing control trials are important for validating IB and ensuring stimuli detectability when attended. This represents disagreement on experimental design adequacy.

Both address Experiment 1 results (C25-C27 in OpenEval, C26-C27 in peer review). OpenEval finds the above-chance performance SUPPORTED with proper statistical analysis. Peer reviewers rate it UNCERTAIN, acknowledging above-chance performance but characterizing it as only a 'modest' overestimate (1.44-8.19%) and questioning whether it proves conscious perception versus subliminal priming.

Both evaluate conservative reporting bias findings. OpenEval R7 addresses C28-C31 including bias evidence (C31), finding it SUPPORTED. Peer R2 addresses C6, C31, C36, C39 about bias, also finding it SUPPORTED. Both agree the bias finding itself is convincing, though peer reviewers dispute its theoretical implications for the nature of IB.

Both address claim C37 about the color congruency effect in Experiment 4. OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED, noting the authors appropriately identified this potential confound. Peer reviewers also implicitly accept it as SUPPORTED, acknowledging the problem and the authors' correction in Experiment 5, though it raised methodological concerns.

OpenEval R12 addresses main findings summary (C5-C7, C61) as SUPPORTED by convergent evidence. Peer R1 includes C5 in their UNCERTAIN evaluation, acknowledging above-chance performance but characterizing the overall effect as modest. Both address the core empirical findings but differ on magnitude and interpretation.

OpenEval R12 includes C6 (conservative bias) in summary of main findings as SUPPORTED. Peer R2 also addresses C6 as SUPPORTED, with the editor explicitly stating authors show participants are conservative and biased. Both agree on this finding, representing a key area of concordance.

OpenEval finds claims C1, C9-C11 about IB as a foundational phenomenon SUPPORTED by extensive citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background/literature characterization claims.

OpenEval finds claims C12-C14, C2-C3 about the orthodox interpretation of IB SUPPORTED as accurately representing the field's dominant view. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this characterization of existing theory.

OpenEval finds claims C38-C40, C87-C89 about Experiment 5 (addressing color congruency confound) SUPPORTED with massive sample size and replication of patterns. No direct peer review evaluation found, though peer R8 acknowledges the motivation for this experiment.

OpenEval finds claims C45, C90, C92 about methodological assumptions (equal variance, log-linear correction) SUPPORTED, noting transparent treatment. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these technical methodological details.

OpenEval finds claims C59-C60, C65 about theoretical reframing toward graded perspective SUPPORTED by pattern of partial sensitivity and confidence-accuracy relationship. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific theoretical proposal.

OpenEval finds claims C50, C64 about methodological contributions and recommendations SUPPORTED, noting the study addresses limitations from prior meta-analysis. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, though peer R7 compliments methodological innovations.

OpenEval finds claims C51-C53 summarizing prior neuroscience and behavioral findings SUPPORTED as accurate literature summary. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these contextual background claims.
